--- Page 72 ---
<meta>This page transitions from a general discussion on spiritual persistence and good works to a specific ritualistic "experiment" for obtaining divine favor or "Grace." Note: there is a discrepancy in page numbering between the previous translation (93) and this transcription (67), but the thematic focus on spiritual labor and the "attainment" of divine assistance remains consistent.</meta>

The experiment of Grace <note>original: "experimentum Gratia"; here "Grace" likely refers to both divine favor and the social "grace" or favor needed to successfully petition a person of higher status</note> is written, concerning which it is said that it requires a pen, ink, and clean paper. It is then said that it should be sprinkled with holy water, and this is how it must be done: let the characters or the names of Grace be written together. Then, it is said that regarding the preservation of these characters, this letter <term>breve: a short written document, often worn as a protective charm or amulet</term> should be placed in a silk cloth, and [the following] is said over it:

->Most holy and most powerful Lord <note>original: "Adonay"</note>, Alpha and Omega <note>The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, representing God as the beginning and the ending of all things</note>, through your mercy—you who are full of mercy and truth—hear my prayers.<-

And afterward it is said: "The mercy of the Lord be upon your truth" <note>original: "Misericordia domine super tua veritate"</note>. Thus the experiment is confirmed and well-preserved by the holy one and the Lord <note>original: "Adonay"</note> who is seen over this letter. Once placed at the perfected time, such a letter ought to remain under the cloth for a day and a night.

## Concerning Fasts and Observance
### chapter four

When the <term>necromancer</term><note>original: "Necromanticus". In this period, the term referred to a ritual magician who works with spirits, rather than the modern sense of a "death mage."</note> wishes to perform his work, and after all preparations have been made, he must first of all foster <term>observance</term><note>original: "custodia". This refers to a state of spiritual "guardianship" or "keeping" one's soul pure through strict discipline.</note> from the very first <term>Beginning</term><note>original: "Inceptione". The formal commencement of a multi-day ritual operation.</note> of choosing the work. He must abstain from all illicit things and every defilement of the body, from excess in food and drink, from all shameful speech and base games, from lust, and from the telling of idle tales. He should maintain as much decency within himself as possible, whether in his speaking, his walking, his drinking, or in all his actions. This must be observed for nearly nine days before the day of the Beginning, and his <term>Disciples</term><note>original: "Discipuli". Assistants who aided the primary magician (the Master) in the complex rituals.</note> must conduct themselves in the same manner. Note that twice or thrice a day, for nine days before the Beginning of the work, the <term>Master</term><note>original: "Magister". The lead practitioner of the rite.</note> and his fellow disciples should say this <term>prayer</term><note>original: "orationem". A formal petition to God to grant the purity and authority needed to command spirits.</note> together, both in the morning and in the evening.

> Lord God Almighty, look upon us your servants who are not worthy to speak your holy name; fill us with the grace of your spirit and enlighten us, for you called the <unclear>Canaanite woman</unclear><note>original: "Cananeam". A reference to the biblical story in Matthew 15, where a Canaanite woman's faith leads to the healing of her daughter.</note> and the publican to repentance and your mercy. Forgive us all our sins. <unclear>I am yours, [for you are the] Father</unclear><note>original: "ego tam sum tuus pater". The Latin here is likely corrupted in the original manuscript or OCR; it likely intended to say "For you are the Father of all creatures."</note> of all your creatures; through your piety and mercy and through the humanity of your clemency, which you have <unclear>offered</unclear> to us sinners, <unclear>you save [us].</unclear>

<meta>This page appears much later in the manuscript than the previous excerpt (page 77). While the earlier text focused on liturgical blessings and the nature of the Divine, this section transitions into moral instruction and practical ethics, specifically focusing on the renunciation of vice and the cultivation of virtue.</meta>

# 795

Therefore, to "say farewell to sins" <note>original: "a peccatis vale dicere"</note> in the common tongue is, first, to renounce <unclear>wicked</unclear> habits on a set day, and even more so afterward, to diligently avoid all occasions of sin—whether of pleasure, or <unclear>living together</unclear>, or those involving the eyes or ears, and finally all of the senses.

This involves turning away from **Pride**, from **Greed**, from that which is as monstrous as it is beastly <note>The author uses "ferina" (beastly), likely referring to animalistic lusts or unrestrained rage</note>, from **Envy**, from **Gluttony**, from **Wrath**, from **Sloth** <term>Ignavia: a lack of spiritual or mental energy; a synonym for the sin of sloth</term> of the soul, and then from idleness, from bad company, from [bad] advice and persuasion, from evil speeches or words, and from places and persons that in any way lead toward sinning and <unclear>offending</unclear>. This applies both to the one who gives himself over to these things and the one who makes others liable to them.

On the contrary, [one must live] by **Humility**, by **Frugality** <term>parsimonia: thrift or moderation in spending and consumption</term>, by **Chastity**, by **Abstinence**, by **Patience**, by **Diligence**, and by **Prudence**. Finally, this is the quality and the precept against those things which are described in the common tongue, namely: [turning away] from [evil] thoughts, from [illicit] pleasure and illusion, from **Ignorance**, from **Weakness**, from all **Malice**, from the giving and receiving of illegal things, from [moral] laxity, from the harboring of evil, and from the deception of others.

Instead, [one follows] the path of obedience—or rather, the turning away from wicked adherence to sins. The precept is: do not detract from the good reputation of your neighbors; do not spread errors regarding their fame; do not diminish their glory or the truth. Truly, do not reveal a secret; do not deceive a friend. Keep the faith of the saints and of your lords; keep your word. Do not take away another's honor, but live with a chaste and pious heart, sharing goods and gifts. And just as one is able to have life by living, do not presume to do harm.

<summary>This page provides a moral framework for "saying farewell to sin," listing specific vices to avoid—such as pride, greed, and bad company—and virtues to embrace, including humility, frugality, and social integrity.</summary>
<keywords>vices and virtues, repentance, social ethics, Seven Deadly Sins, moral discipline, neighborly conduct</keywords>

...through human frailty <note>original: "humana fragilitate." A common theological term referring to the inherent weakness of human nature that leads to sin.</note> against God and my neighbor,
whether in thought or speech, whether by acting, or by taking pleasure,

have taken up [arms] and I had committed iniquity against my God; through all things
I confess to Him, just as those who rejoice in your mercy
and do not boast, and [I confess] of your justice to you, God the judge.

witness; but concerning joy, I shall speak of that to you through your justice.

of which the face of many speaks.
Holy Lord, Father and merciful one, who created all things
and who knows and recognizes everything, and [whose] regard looks upon man.

Regarding the first point, it must be observed that no one can provide testimony concerning the facts of a business matter, the legal rights of a property, or the personal character <term>qualitate personae: the status, reputation, or legal standing of an individual</term> of anyone, unless they first possess knowledge of those facts, rights, or personal qualities about which they are testifying. ### In what manner circles are made
### and how one should work within them

### Chapter Nine

How circles are made—namely three or more—in the place where the circle is to be made, with all its necessities, equipment <term>paramentis; ritual tools or ceremonial garments</term>, knives, and experiments <note>original: *experimentis*; in medieval grimoires, this term refers to specific magical procedures or spells rather than scientific trials</note>.

Take the aforementioned knife in hand and dig into the earth in the middle of the place where you wish to make the circle. Afterward, take a cord, and from the center of that circle, extend it into four parts toward the four quarters of the world—that is, the regions of the world: the south, the east, the west, the south <note>The original text repeats "meridiem" (south), which may be a scribe's error for the general four-fold orientation</note>, and the north. No other person [should be present] during this work. In the middle, place two swords <term>enses; ritual blades used to command spirits or define sacred space</term>, specifically the one you wish to use with the stated knife, or from the upper and northern part, marking <unclear>prohibiting</unclear> and indicating a cross to the right with the knife. You shall make another circle in its entirety with the said knife, and always dividing by individual sections, you shall make a circle between them at a distance of half a foot.

--- Page 114 ---
<meta>This page provides specific ritual instructions for the creation and consecration of candles used in magical operations. It continues the theme of "Lights and Hours" established on earlier pages, moving from general titles to practical applications.</meta>

It must be noted whether the work is to be by day or by night, one must have lights
either for performing the work or for reading and for performing the 
necessary consecrations, so that the lights 
must be made when any work ought to be performed,
whether by day or by night; and let there be a candle or lights
made by day, specifically on the day of Mercury <note>original: "die Mercurij"; Wednesday</note> and in its hour, during a waxing moon;
and they ought to be prepared and afterward they ought to be stored in a 
clean silk cloth, and they must be worked with "new fire" <note>original: "igne novo"; fire freshly kindled, usually with flint and steel, rather than taken from an existing flame</note>, a small bright 
spark or fire, and the work should be performed with such a candle.
First, on the day of Mercury in its hour, take thread 
spun by a virgin girl <note>original: "puella virgines filatum"; a common requirement in medieval magic to ensure the purity and "untouched" nature of ritual materials</note>, and let it be on a wooden [mold], and upon 
that material let thick candles be made, the size of an arm or 
a cord, weighing half a pound, and when they have been made, 
let these characters be written upon them here and there: <note>The manuscript contains a series of occult or astrological sigils including a cross, a crescent moon with dots, and stylized characters resembling the letters 'h', 'o', and 'u'.</note> and afterward it is said—
afterward let him say six psalms over the candles: "Bless the Lord, all 
you works of the Lord" <note>The *Benedicite*, or Song of the Three Young Men</note>. "Bless the Lord, O my soul" <note>Psalm 103 or 104</note>. 
"Praise the Lord, all you nations" <note>Psalm 117</note> and "We praise thee, O God" <note>The *Te Deum*</note>
and the "Sanctification of the Lord Jesus Christ," etc. But first 
let it be proclaimed "In the name of the Father," etc. Amen. Furthermore, 
let it be said: "I exorcise you, creature of wax <note>original: "creatura cere"</note>, by Him who created all things 
from nothing, so that you may be so visible <note>interpreted as "spiritually potent" or "revealing"</note> that every 
phantom <note>original: "phantasma"; an illusory spirit or deceptive vision</note> and every deceit [may flee], and may the power 
of the Most High be in you, and may it be able to illuminate all things, so that nothing [remains hidden], in the name [of...].

<summary>This page outlines the ritual construction of magical candles, requiring they be made on a Wednesday during a waxing moon using thread spun by a virgin. The process includes inscribing sigils and performing an exorcism of the wax to dispel illusions and phantoms.</summary>
<keywords>ritual magic, candles, Mercury, waxing moon, virgin-spun thread, exorcism of wax, phantoms, sigils, consecration</keywords>

From whatever day and hour, but only on the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday</note> for the purpose [of this ritual], on the said day you must prepare the exorcised knife <term>cultrum: a ceremonial blade, often used in medieval magic to carve sigils or cut ritual parchment</term> and leave it in the sun for one day; thus thereafter for a certain time, at one hour with the same knife on the same day and hour, you shall place these characters <term>characteres: magical sigils or planetary signs</term> upon the knife, on one side and on the other:

--- Page 138 ---
<meta>This page marks a significant shift in the manuscript from the practical geometry and instrument-making of the previous pages to a philosophical and metaphysical discussion. It begins a new section regarding the nature of "spirits"—a term that in this period could refer to biological vapors, the breath, or the soul itself.</meta>

# Treatise on spirits
## and their nature
### divided into three chapters

## Chapter one
### On the nature of spirits.

Air is a corruptible <term>element<note>original: "elementum corruptibile". In the science of this period, "corruptible" does not mean "evil," but rather "subject to change and decay," a property of all things found on Earth as opposed to the unchanging heavens.</note></term> throughout its whole, externally mobile, indivisible, and capable of receiving quantity; it is a smoky moisture and exists beneath the composite whole. For this reason, it is said that what is called "spirit" <note>original: "spiritus"</note> is what the intellectual soul is said to be—called nothing else but spirit, or what is called "living air." It comes from God just like light; just as light is said to be called <unclear>is</unclear> spirit. These are the elements according to the <unclear>earth</unclear> itself, endowed by God with its changing qualities. Thus it is carried, as if among the elements, by the influence of the planets into the earth, having emerged from the heart; it is simply called a thing which is indeed called light, and is so called in tribulation. And even if it is not granted to every place, it is called spirit equally for those <unclear>disposed</unclear> towards it; wherefore, whatever of their own <unclear>disposition</unclear> they are given for their work, the earth holds the spirit; equally, the spirit is then said to be from God, who speaks forever.

<summary>This page begins a new treatise defining "spirit" as a divine substance related to air and light, influenced by planetary movements and the intellectual soul. It characterizes air as a "living" element that mediates between God and the physical world.</summary>
<keywords>spirit, nature of air, intellectual soul, planetary influence, divine light, elements, metaphysics</keywords>

### On the Duties of Prelates <note>A "prelate" is a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop, abbot, or superior, who exercises jurisdiction.</note>

#### On Successors

#### Chapter Two

->It is necessary for prelates to act honorably when choosing those<-
->successors who are to be designated. For indeed, they are not<-
->like those who desire successors to be chosen and<-
->designated for selfish reasons. Sometimes there are good qualities in the candidates<-
->which are not present in the ones choosing them. Therefore, they should not<-
->accept them out of personal favoritism <note>original: "gratia," referring to partiality or choosing someone to gain favor</note>. And this is what is<-
->meant by the saying: "They undertake these duties faithfully and honorably." They desire them<-
->because they are good; because they are fit to be prelates; because<-
->they are honorable. Therefore, they ought not to receive them<-
->out of favoritism. And this is what is said.<-

<summary>This page outlines the ethical standards for high-ranking clergy when appointing their successors, emphasizing that candidates should be chosen for their virtue and merit rather than through corruption or personal favoritism.</summary>
<keywords>prelates, succession, clerical ethics, ecclesiastical office, favoritism, merit, corruption</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on the ethical selection of successors within the Church to a broader discussion of secular leadership, specifically focusing on the reciprocal relationship between a ruler and their subjects.</meta>

## On Gratitude toward Subjects

### Chapter Three

Because a King and Prince <note>In this context, "Prince" refers generally to a sovereign ruler or head of state.</note> administers his rule well not only through his own efforts but also through his subjects, he must therefore conduct himself toward them with a sense of reciprocity. As Ctesias <note>A Greek physician and historian from the 5th century BCE who wrote "Persica," a history of Assyria and Persia.</note> reports, if the King of the Persians knew that he would gain both utility and praise through gratitude toward his subjects, he would practice this by providing for them, protecting them, and appointing to their proper stations <note>original: "in proprio loco ponendo," meaning assigning roles or offices based on merit and status</note> whoever he judged worthy of his favor, according to their character and honor. He would grant them dignity and affection to increase their renown, showing favor and singular goodwill, thereby preserving the immortal memory of these men; for the King is said to celebrate their persons with honors and clearly through formal proclamations <note>original: "instrumentis," which likely refers to official decrees or the ceremonial "tools" of state governance</note>, as well as with great and generous gifts. On the other hand, the gratitude shown by the subjects consists of their obedience in their required service, their vigilance, their constancy, and their effort to act faithfully in every deed.

->**Gratitude**, **King of the Persians**, **Ctesias**,<-
->**Prince**, **Subjects**, **Rule**<-

<summary>This page discusses the necessity of mutual gratitude between a ruler and their subjects, using the King of the Persians as a historical model for rewarding merit and loyalty to ensure stable governance.</summary>
<keywords>kingship, subjects, gratitude, Ctesias, Persian Empire, reciprocity, governance, merit</keywords>
